title: The Mind Shorts
chapters: Boredom: the feeling we'll do almost anything to escape
Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke

units.t: The Mind Shorts.
In this episode: Boredom: the feeling we'll do almost anything to escape and Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke.
Part one. Boredom: the feeling we'll do almost anything to escape.
Given the choice between sitting quietly with their thoughts and giving themselves an electric shock, many people chose the shock.
What is boredom trying to tell us?
Shock or sit still.

In studies published in 2014, psychologist Timothy Wilson and colleagues at the University of Virginia asked people to sit alone in a plain room for about six to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think.
No phone, no book, no pen.
Many found it unpleasant.
In one version, participants had first been given a mild electric shock, and many said they would pay money to avoid feeling it again.
Yet when left alone with a button that would deliver the same shock, about two thirds of men and a quarter of women pressed it at least once.
One participant pressed it 190 times.
The result raised a question: what exactly is boredom?
A signal, not a flaw.
Boredom is not the same as having nothing to do.
You can relax happily on a beach, and you can be bored stiff in a meeting while busy.
In 2012, psychologist John Eastwood and colleagues defined it as 'the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity'.
The mind is ready to be used, but the situation, perhaps too easy, too hard or meaningless, offers nothing to capture it.
Many researchers now see boredom as a useful emotion, like hunger or pain.
Andreas Elpidorou describes it as a regulatory signal that nudges us towards goals that matter.
It is not laziness or a moral failing.
Boredom and creativity.
A popular idea says boredom makes us more creative.
In a 2014 study, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman had some participants copy numbers from a phone book.
Afterwards, they thought of more uses for a pair of plastic cups than people who had not been bored.
The theory is that when the world is dull, the mind wanders and makes unexpected connections.
It is an appealing finding, but the studies have been small and results across experiments have been mixed.
Some mind-wandering time may help creativity, but treating boredom as a guaranteed creativity booster goes beyond the evidence.
Proneness and phones.
People differ in how often they get bored.
Since Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg developed a Boredom Proneness Scale in 1986, researchers have found that easily bored people report more attention problems, impulsive behaviour and low mood.
Boredom proneness has also been linked with gambling, overeating and substance use, perhaps because these offer quick stimulation.
These are associations, not proof that boredom causes the problems.
Smartphones offer an instant escape from even a few seconds of boredom.
If boredom signals us to seek something meaningful, endless scrolling may silence the signal without satisfying it.
Whether phones make us more bored overall is not settled, but a mindless scroll rarely leaves people refreshed.
Making boredom work.
If boredom is a signal, listen to it.
Ask what is missing: challenge, meaning, novelty or control.
A task that is too easy can become a game, such as beating your previous time.
A task that is too hard may need breaking into smaller steps.
If something feels pointless, connect it to a goal you care about.
It is also worth occasionally letting yourself be bored without escaping, such as walking without headphones or sitting with a cup of tea and no screen.
Many people find that ideas, plans and solutions surface in those quiet gaps.
Boredom, used well, can be the start of something interesting.
The key idea: Many people find being alone with their thoughts so unpleasant that they would rather give themselves a mild electric shock.
Part two. Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke.
You got the job, passed the exam or won the award, and you're quietly waiting to be found out.
You are in very good company.
Waiting to be found out.
Picture a doctor newly qualified, a manager freshly promoted, or a student who topped the class.
From the outside they look confident.
Inside runs a different story: 'I got lucky.
Any day now, someone will realise I don't know what I'm doing.'
This feeling of being a fraud despite clear evidence of competence is widely known as impostor syndrome.
The concept was introduced in 1978 by American psychologists Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes, working with high-achieving women who credited luck or charm rather than ability.
Note the word phenomenon, not syndrome.
It is not a mental illness or a diagnosis.
It describes thoughts and feelings many ordinary, healthy people experience at times.
Later research found it in men as well, across many professions and cultures.
How common is it.
You may have seen claims that 70 per cent of people experience impostor feelings.
That figure is repeated often, but its origins are murky.
A 2020 systematic review led by Dena Bravata found reported rates from under ten per cent to over eighty per cent, depending on who was studied and how it was measured.
The honest conclusion is that nobody knows the exact figure, but impostor feelings are very common, particularly during transitions such as starting university, a new job or a promotion.
They seem especially frequent among people who are among the first in their family or community to reach a particular position, and in competitive fields where everyone around you seems brilliant.
The impostor cycle.
Clance described a self-sustaining loop sometimes called the impostor cycle.
Faced with a task, a person feels anxious and doubtful.
They respond in one of two ways: by overpreparing, working far longer than necessary, or by procrastinating, then working frantically at the last minute.
The task goes well.
But instead of concluding 'I'm good at this', they explain the success away.
If they overprepared, it was only the extra effort.
If they procrastinated, it was luck.
Either way, the success does not count as evidence of ability, so the doubt is ready and waiting for the next task.
Breaking the cycle often starts with noticing how you explain your wins, and whether you would accept that explanation from a friend.
Not a skill problem.
Impostor feelings are sometimes described as the opposite of the Dunning-Kruger effect, the idea that people with low skill overestimate themselves.
The comparison is catchy but loose.
People with impostor feelings are usually genuinely competent.
Expertise can even feed the feeling: the more you learn, the more you see how much you don't know, while beginners may be blissfully unaware of the gaps.
Some researchers also criticise the 'syndrome' label for putting all the focus on individuals.

If you are the only person like you in a room, hear subtle comments questioning whether you belong, or never see anyone with your background in senior roles, feeling out of place may be a reasonable response to real signals.
Leaders should ask what the environment is communicating, not just tell people to be more confident.
Quieting the inner critic.
Several simple habits loosen the grip of impostor feelings.
Talk about it: hearing that respected colleagues feel the same is powerfully reassuring.
Keep a record of positive feedback, results and things you have learned, and reread it when doubts flare.
Separate feelings from facts by asking, 'What evidence would convince me I'm competent?'
and checking whether it already exists.
Accept that not knowing everything is normal at every level.
Mentors can tell you what 'good' looks like in your field.
If self-doubt is persistent, affecting your sleep or mood, or stopping you from going for opportunities, it is worth speaking to your GP.
This is general information, not personal advice, and healthdirect and Beyond Blue have useful resources.
The key idea: Many capable people secretly believe they don't deserve their success, a pattern named in 1978 as the impostor phenomenon.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did the 2014 study find about being alone with one's thoughts?
Answer. Many found it unpleasant, and some chose to shock themselves.
Question two. Why is 'impostor phenomenon' the more accurate term than 'syndrome'?
Answer. It is a pattern of thoughts and feelings, not a diagnosis.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
